attack.title: Login
attack.description: User-controlled credentials are concatenated into a SQL statement, so input can change the statement's meaning.
attack.objective: Explain how an injection flaw in an authentication query can become an authentication bypass.
attack.defense: Use parameterized SQL and treat authentication as a separate control from input validation.

attack.title: Home
attack.description: The application accepts a session identifier chosen by the requester instead of generating and rotating it at a trust-boundary change.
attack.objective: Describe why accepting an attacker-chosen session identifier can let an attacker predict a victim's authenticated session.
attack.defense: Generate session identifiers server-side and rotate them after authentication or privilege changes.

attack.title: Profile
attack.description: Possession of the session identifier is sufficient to impersonate the user, and the application exposes weak session handling around that identifier.
attack.objective: Relate browser cookies, server-side session state, and impersonation when a session token is stolen or replayed.
attack.defense: Use high-entropy rotated tokens, appropriate cookie attributes, short lifetimes, and explicit logout/invalidation.

attack.title: Users
attack.description: The id parameter is concatenated directly into SQL, allowing data to be interpreted as executable query syntax.
attack.objective: Predict how changing an input value changes the SQL statement and the rows returned by the database.
attack.defense: Use parameterized SQL and validate the expected data type before querying.

attack.title: Message
attack.description: Untrusted input is inserted into an HTML response without context-appropriate output encoding.
attack.objective: Distinguish data from executable browser content and explain why output context determines the required encoding.
attack.defense: Apply context-appropriate output encoding and use a restrictive Content Security Policy as defense in depth.

attack.title: Guestbook
attack.description: Comments are stored safely as database values but later emitted into HTML without output encoding.
attack.objective: Explain why safe database insertion does not prevent stored XSS when output is later rendered unsafely.
attack.defense: Encode untrusted values when they are rendered into HTML; input validation alone is not an XSS defense.

attack.title: Jump
attack.description: The redirect target is taken directly from user input, so a trusted application URL can send a user to an attacker-chosen destination.
attack.owasp: Related to A01:2025 Broken Access Control
attack.objective: Explain how unvalidated redirects can support phishing and trust-boundary confusion even without code execution.
attack.defense: Prefer server-side identifiers for destinations or allow only validated local paths.

attack.title: Extract
attack.evil_path: Generated by the application at risk level 3
attack.description: Python pickle can invoke callable behavior while reconstructing objects, so deserializing attacker-controlled pickle data can execute code.
attack.owasp: A08:2025 Software or Data Integrity Failures
attack.objective: Explain why serialization formats that can encode executable behavior must not be accepted across an untrusted boundary.
attack.defense: Use a non-executable data format with explicit schema validation, such as JSON for simple data structures.

attack.title: Diagnostics
attack.evil_path: Generated for the host operating system at risk level 3
attack.description: The domain value is concatenated into a shell command and executed with shell=True, allowing shell metacharacters to introduce additional commands.
attack.objective: Identify the boundary between command arguments and shell syntax, and explain how shell=True changes that boundary.
attack.defense: Avoid the shell, pass arguments as a list, and validate values against the expected domain-name grammar.

attack.title: Documents
attack.description: The application resolves a requester-controlled path without constraining the resulting file to an intended document directory.
attack.objective: Use canonical paths to explain why checking a string before path resolution is weaker than checking the resolved location.
attack.defense: Resolve paths under a fixed base directory, reject paths that escape it, and keep URL fetching separate from file access.

attack.title: Admin
attack.description: The application sends client-side navigation instructions but continues to include protected content in the same response.
attack.objective: Explain why authorization must decide whether protected data is generated, not merely where the browser navigates afterward.
attack.defense: Perform server-side authorization before generating protected content and return immediately on denial.

attack.title: Settings
attack.evil_path: Submit a cross-origin request that changes the email field
attack.description: A state-changing operation trusts ambient session cookies and has no anti-CSRF token or origin validation.
attack.objective: Explain why authentication cookies identify the browser session but do not prove that the user intended a particular state-changing request.
attack.defense: Use non-GET state changes, anti-CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies, and origin checks as appropriate.

attack.title: Danger
attack.evil_path: Frame /danger in an attacker-controlled page and visually disguise the delete button
attack.description: The application permits framing and places a destructive action where a user can be tricked into clicking through an overlay.
attack.owasp: Related to A01:2025 Broken Access Control
attack.objective: Explain how UI redressing can cause an authenticated user to invoke an action they did not intend.
attack.defense: Use CSP frame-ancestors or X-Frame-Options and require deliberate confirmation for destructive actions.
